title: A Message Within Reach
overview: Paul, grieving that many of his fellow Jews have not accepted Jesus, argues that God's way of making people right with him comes through trusting Christ, is open to everyone, and is already within reach.

parts.label: Paul's longing for his people (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Paul, himself Jewish, prays for his fellow Israelites and says they are truly devoted to God, but he believes they have missed what God was doing in Jesus. He calls Christ the law's goal or end point; the Greek word can mean either, which is why translations differ and interpreters weigh both senses.

parts.label: Not out of reach (vv. 5-8)
parts.note: Paul quotes Moses on living by keeping the law, then borrows Moses' words in Deuteronomy that God's command was not hidden up in the sky or far across the sea. He applies them to Christ: no one has to climb to heaven or go down among the dead to fetch him, because God has already sent him and raised him.

parts.label: Mouth and heart (vv. 9-13)
parts.note: Saying aloud that Jesus is Lord was a public statement of loyalty, and trusting that God raised him is its inner side; together they echo the mouth and heart of the verse just quoted, not two separate steps. The promise that everyone who calls on the Lord will be saved comes from the prophet Joel, where it meant Israel's God, and Paul seems to apply it to Jesus and open it to Jews and non-Jews alike.

parts.label: Someone has to tell them (vv. 14-15)
parts.note: Paul builds a chain backward: calling on God needs trust, trust needs hearing, hearing needs a messenger, and a messenger needs to be sent. The line about beautiful feet comes from Isaiah, where it welcomed runners bringing news of the exiles' return from Babylon, and Paul uses it for those spreading the news about Jesus.

parts.label: Did they not hear? (vv. 16-18)
parts.note: Paul admits many did not accept the message and points to Isaiah's own complaint that few believed. His quote about voices reaching the whole earth comes from a psalm about the sky declaring God's glory, and scholars are unsure whether he meant it as prophecy or simply borrowed fitting words.

parts.label: Outsiders welcomed, hands still open (vv. 19-21)
parts.note: Using Moses and Isaiah, Paul argues that Israel's own scriptures foresaw God being found by outsiders, which would stir Israel to jealousy. The closing image is harsh about Israel's refusal, yet it shows God still reaching out all day long, and in the next chapter Paul insists God has not rejected his people.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the righteousness Paul says his people tried to establish for themselves means trying to earn God's approval by good works or relying on Jewish identity and law keeping as the mark of God's people, which shapes how they read his whole contrast between law and faith.
think: Have you ever been deeply committed to something and later come to see it differently, and what helped you see it?
